title: Checklist for Auditors: A Practical Guide From Scoping to Closure
summary: A practical checklist for auditors: scope, evidence, testing, findings with the five Cs, reporting and follow-up, built on ISO, IIA, GAO and AICPA guidance.
body_markdown:
A good checklist for auditors follows the life of an engagement: understand why the audit exists, scope it, plan the evidence, test the controls, document findings, report, and confirm that fixes actually happened. We walk through each stage below, with the questions to ask at every step, so you can adapt it to an internal audit, a SOC 2 examination or a vendor security review.

## TL;DR


- Use a checklist as a planning and note-taking tool built for the specific audit, not a generic form that restricts your judgment.
- Work in six stages: purpose and scope, evidence plan, control testing, findings, reporting, follow-up.
- Structure every finding with the five Cs: criterion, condition, consequence, cause, corrective action.
- Collect evidence continuously. Assembling months of evidence in the final week is a common cause of overruns.
- Close high-risk items with independent validation, not management self-certification alone.

## What an audit checklist is, and what it is for


An audit checklist is a work document that lists what the auditor will examine, ask and verify. ISO 19011 names checklists among the[work documents audit team members may prepare](https://committee.iso.org/files/live/sites/tc176sc2/files/documents/ISO%209001%20Auditing%20Practices%20Group%20docs/Auditing%20General/APG-Checklist2015.pdf) , and the ISO 9001 Auditing Practices Group adds that they should not restrict audit activities, which may change as information is collected.


Used well, a checklist built for one audit does several jobs at once. According to the same ISO guidance, it promotes planning, keeps the approach consistent, acts as a sampling plan and time manager, serves as a memory aid, and holds the notes you collect along the way.


### Is a checklist required?


Not always. The ISO guidance says checklists are one tool in the auditor's toolbox, and whether to use one depends on customer needs, time and cost, auditor experience and sector scheme requirements. It also warns that a generic checklist that does not reflect the organization's management system may add no value and can interfere with the audit. So treat the template below as a starting frame and tailor each line to the organization in front of you.


## Stage 1: Understand the purpose and define the scope


Before fieldwork, the team should understand why the project is on the audit plan. The[Audit Management Playbook](https://b2saas.com/uploads/topics/files/auditboard/1.pdf) suggests answering, and getting approval for, questions such as why the project was approved, how the process supports organizational goals, which enterprise risks it addresses and whether significant changes have occurred.


Then set boundaries. For a SOC examination at a software company,[Deloitte's SOC readiness guide](https://www.deloitte.com/content/dam/assets-zone3/us/en/docs/services/audit-assurance/2026/tpa-soc-readiness-in-practice-V6.pdf) advises identifying the systems, products, services, locations, processes and criteria that may be included, and considering intended report users, subservice organizations, key technologies and exclusions.


**Scoping checklist**


1. Confirm the reason the audit was approved and the outcome required.
2. Align stakeholders and name a control owner for each area.
3. List in-scope systems, products, services, locations and processes.
4. Record exclusions and limitations in writing.
5. Identify subservice organizations and who will read the report.
6. Map data flows and control processes.
7. Agree the timeline and the resources the engagement needs.


PwC's guidance on[establishing an examination strategy](https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/aicpav2/aag-cyb/aag-cyb/aag-cyb2/aag-cyb_establishing_an_overall_examination.html) , which references AT-C section 205A, adds that the practitioner should ascertain reporting objectives and the nature, timing and extent of resources required.


## Stage 2: Build the audit program and evidence plan


An audit program turns scope into testable steps. The Audit Management Playbook says it should detail process objectives, process risks, the controls that mitigate them, and control attributes: preventive or detective, frequency, manual or automated, fraud relevance and an initial risk assessment. Testing procedures include inquiry, observation, inspection and re-performance.


The European Court of Auditors' guide on[designing audit procedures](https://methodology.eca.europa.eu/aware/GAP/Pages/CA-FA/Planning/Designing-audit-procedures.aspx) gives a useful template for each line of your checklist:


Element What to write down


Requirement The rule, regulation or criterion being tested


Risk The assessed risk it relates to


Key controls Controls expected to address the risk


Audit steps Evidence to obtain, work to perform, procedure type


Conclusion Result against the objective, or further testing if negative


### Plan evidence early


Jacobian Engineering's[SOC 2 guide for SaaS companies](https://jacobianengineering.com/resources/whitepapers/soc-2-compliance-trust-services-criteria-saas-guide) calls late evidence collection, trying to assemble six months of evidence in the last week before fieldwork, the most common cause of audit overruns, and recommends automating collection from day one. The same guide describes a readiness phase of roughly weeks 1 to 4 for gap analysis and a fieldwork phase of 4 to 6 weeks for a mid-sized SaaS company.


The same discipline applies in regulated screening. Records that must survive scrutiny are easiest to defend when they are packaged as they are created, as with[audit-ready evidence bundles](https://prehirebadge.com/features/evidence-bundles) for background-check adverse actions.


## Stage 3: Test security, risk and internal controls


What to review depends on the standard, but the IIA's[Cybersecurity Topical Requirement](https://internalauditor.theiia.org/globalassets/site/standards/topical-requirements/cybersecurity/cybersecurity_topical_requirement.pdf) gives a solid map of three areas internal auditors must assess.


**Governance**


- Cybersecurity strategy
- Policies and procedures
- Roles and responsibilities
- Stakeholder engagement


**Risk management**


- Identifying, analyzing, mitigating and monitoring threats
- Escalation processes
- Incident response and recovery


**Control processes**


- Internal and vendor controls
- Talent management and continuous monitoring
- IT asset life cycle, configuration, encryption and patching
- User-access management
- Network controls and endpoint communication security


In a cybersecurity risk management examination, PwC notes that entity-level controls usually map to the trust services criteria for communication and information (CC2.1 to 2.3), risk assessment (CC3.1 to 3.4) and monitoring (CC4.1 to 4.2), following a top-down approach. If your audit is a SOC 2, our guide to[SOC 2 requirements](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/soc-2-compliance-requirements-your-2026-guide) and our[SOC 2 compliance checklist](https://skypher.co/post/soc-2-compliance-checklist-7-steps-en) go deeper on control areas.


### Document what you tested


PwC's documentation guidance, referencing AU-C section 230, says audit documentation should let an experienced auditor with no previous connection to the audit understand the procedures performed, the evidence obtained, significant findings, conclusions and professional judgments. Add a line to your checklist for each item: what was tested, how, what evidence, what conclusion.


## Stage 4: Write findings with the five Cs


A finding that cannot be acted on is a wasted finding. The Chartered IIA describes the[five Cs](https://charterediia.org/content-hub/blogs/use-of-the-five-cs-in-communication/) for structuring findings and recommendations:


1. **Criterion:** the standard or control that should be in place.
2. **Condition:** what you observed.
3. **Consequence:** the risk or effect.
4. **Cause:** the root cause.
5. **Corrective action:** the recommendation or management's plan.


The U.S. Government Accountability Office's[Yellow Book](https://www.gao.gov/assets/d24106786.pdf) defines the elements of a finding as criteria, condition, cause and effect. The IIA's[five attributes article](https://internalauditor.theiia.org/en/articles/2023/february/the-five-attributes-approach/) calls effect the "so what" and cause the attribute auditors most often under-address, so spend extra time there.


Place findings in perspective too. Guidance on government auditing findings says to describe the nature and extent of issues and relate instances to the population or number of cases examined. "3 of 25 sampled access reviews were late" is more useful than "access reviews are sometimes late."


## Stage 5: Report and follow up


Reporting ends the fieldwork, not the audit. Capture each observation, the agreed corrective action, an owner and a status. The IIA's guidance on[monitoring progress](https://www.theiia.org/en/content/guidance/recommended/implementation/2500-monitoring-progress/) stresses this record and the chief audit executive's responsibility for monitoring results.


**Follow-up checklist**


- For nonconformities under ISO 9001, confirm there is objective evidence for[correction, cause analysis and corrective action](https://www.iso.org/files/live/sites/tc176sc2/files/documents/ISO%209001%20Auditing%20Practices%20Group%20docs/Auditing%20General/APG-ReviewNonconformity2015.pdf) , and check the fix does not create new problems.
- Separate immediate correction from systemic corrective action, and write SMART commitments. The[SPI guidebook](https://sp-i.org/downloads/spi-10.pdf) suggests plans due by day 30, implementation by day 60 to 90, then effectiveness verification and closure.
- Under the IIA's 2024 Global Internal Audit Standards, Standard 15.2 requires confirming that management[implemented recommendations or action plans](https://trustedinstitute.com/concept/iia-crma/communicating-risk-management-assurance/monitoring-and-follow-up-of-engagement-results/) .
- Make follow-up risk-based: independent validation for high-risk observations, management representation backed by evidence for low-risk ones. Self-certification alone is generally insufficient for high-risk items.

## FAQ


### What is an audit checklist?


It is a working document listing the items an auditor plans to examine, the evidence to obtain and the questions to ask. Per ISO guidance, it supports planning, consistency, sampling and note-taking, but should never restrict the audit.


### What are the five Cs of an audit finding?


Criterion, condition, consequence, cause and corrective action. Together they state what should be true, what you found, why it matters, why it happened and how to fix it.


### Is an audit checklist required?


Not generally. ISO's auditing practices group describes checklists as one tool among several, and the decision depends on customer needs, time, auditor experience and sector requirements. Tailored checklists add more value than generic ones.


### How do auditors verify that corrective actions are complete?


They confirm objective evidence that the fix was implemented and works. Follow-up is risk-based: high-risk items get independent validation, while low-risk items may close on management representation supported by evidence.
